summary: Maine light on a small island at Rockport Harbor: established 1850, rebuilt 1874-75, discontinued 1933; privately owned, grounds and tower closed to visitors.

lens.order: 4 (1856, per LighthouseFriends); a 1902 fifth-to-fourth exchange is also reported and conflicts

structures.note: Built 1874-75 (NRHP); replaced the lantern on the 1850 dwelling
Original 1850 brick front block; square frame ell added 1874-75 (NRHP)
Stone oil house north of the tower (NRHP)
Gable-roofed shed of two connected parts, date not known (NRHP)

access.note: Privately owned; grounds, dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends); USLHS: not open to the public

events.note: Congress appropriates $3,500 on 3 March 1849 for a light at Beauchamp Point or the harbor entrance, at the behest of E. K. Smart
Brick dwelling with a lantern on its roof; station established
Light shown from a lantern on the roof of the brick dwelling
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaces the station's multiple lamps and reflectors (LighthouseFriends). A 1902 fifth-to-fourth exchange is reported too; the two conflict
Lighthouse Board recommends discontinuing the light in November 1857 (as LighthouseFriends quotes it: two miles south of Negro Island light, of no use to general navigation)
Discontinued in 1859 per LighthouseFriends; nomination says deactivated before the 1861 Light List, reason unknown
Congress allocates $9,000 on 23 June 1874; dwelling repaired and a brick tower built 1874-75
Rebuilt complex back in service 15 January 1875 under keeper Joseph Small
David S. Arey appointed keeper, vice Knott C. Perry, deceased (Portland Daily Press, 25 June 1894)
Fiscal year ended 30 June 1900: about 130 feet of boat slip built; minor repairs (Board report). LighthouseFriends dates a 150-foot slip to 1885 instead
LighthouseFriends: fifth-order Fresnel exchanged for a fourth-order lens to increase the light's power; conflicts with the 1856 entry
Keeper C. E. B. Stanley towed a disabled power boat with one man aboard to port, fiscal year ended 30 June 1921
NRHP: the station was sold in 1932
Discontinued 30 June 1933 (LighthouseFriends). The USLHS record gives 1934 as the year discontinued; the nomination says sold in 1932
Sold at auction in September 1934 for $1,025, in a batch of nine abandoned Maine lights (LighthouseFriends)
An automated light was established on Lowell Rock, just off Indian Island: a separate structure, noted here as context only

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record has 1850 (Rowlett, USLHS) and 1875 (Wikidata). The nomination treats 1850 as the establishment, with the first light from a lantern on the brick dwelling, and 1875 as the rebuilt tower's first light after the 1874 appropriation. These are two events, not a contradiction.

corrections.why: LighthouseFriends says the light was discontinued on 30 June 1933 and the island was sold at auction in September 1934. The nomination says the station was sold in 1932. The USLHS record gives 1934 as year discontinued. The sources disagree; this is a human-review item, not a settled correction.

notes_for_editor: DATES OF DISCONTINUANCE AND SALE: nomination says sold 1932; LighthouseFriends says discontinued 30 June 1933 and sold at auction September 1934 for $1,025; USLHS record says discontinued 1934; the station record (Rowlett) says deactivated 1934. Not resolved; the story prints the conflict. LENS: LighthouseFriends gives a fourth-order Fresnel in 1856 and a 1902 exchange of a fifth-order for a fourth-order lens; these cannot both stand as written. The story prints the conflict and gives no order as settled. ISLAND SIZE: LighthouseFriends says seven-acre Indian Island; the nomination's boundary is 4.5 acres and says that includes the entire land mass of the island. Both are printed. FIRST LIGHT: 1850 (establishment) and 1875 (rebuilt light) are both in the sources. KEEPER NAMES: LighthouseFriends spells David Sargent; the USLHS roster spells Sargeant; the roster prints LeRoy Elwell and LighthouseFriends Leroy Elwell; the roster prints William F. Reed and LighthouseFriends William Foster Reed. Roster stints are the archive's, not checked against NARA registers. PRIVATE PERSONS: the 1934 purchaser, the keepers' wife and the granddaughter who recalled the station (via Lighthouse Digest) are deliberately not named. The 1857 Board recommendation of discontinuance is known only through LighthouseFriends' quotation; the Board's 1857 report is not in the local corpus, so the story attributes it to LighthouseFriends. The 1874 plan is likewise attributed to LighthouseFriends' quotation of the Board. The Portland Daily Press item gives the appointment as made on the Saturday before 25 June 1894; the Treasury record was not read. The Knott C. Perry death notice is quoted by LighthouseFriends from an undated local paper; not located in Chronicling America, so it is footnoted to LighthouseFriends. THE STANLEY TOW: the Commissioner's list of rescues is dated to the fiscal year ended 30 June 1921 (the list is headed 'during the fiscal year'); the Bulletin 1918-1923 index (p. 37, which points to Bulletin page 180) also records a tow by Stanley at Indian Island. The story gives the fiscal year, not a calendar date. No storm, wreck or other rescue at this station appears in the sources used. The record's tower height (9.5 m) and characteristic (Fl R 6s) were not confirmed by any source read; the story gives neither. BOAT SLIP: the Board's 1900 report records about 130 feet of boat slip built that year; LighthouseFriends dates a 150-foot boat slip to 1885. Both are printed. TOPOGRAPHY: the Board's 1894 report (scan p. 352) lists Indian Island among the stations where topographical surveys were made; the Board's repair list for the same volume also includes the station. NEWSPAPERS: Chronicling America searches for Indian Island terms returned unrelated Portland pages; only the Perry-succession item is used. The Lowell Rock automated light is a separate structure and appears in the story only as context. KEEPER-NAME TIE: the Bulletin 1918-1923 index entry reads 'Stanley, Charles E.B., keeper Indian Island, tows boat'. The index does not say Maine; another Indian Island (Spit) is in California. The tie to this station rests on the keeper's name matching the Maine keeper C. E. B. Stanley (Commissioner volume and roster); the story cites the index only as recording a tow by Stanley at Indian Island. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-22: the 1894 topographical list ('36. Indian Island') and the 1918-1923 index entry were read from OCR text; the page images were not viewed. The index entry does not name the state; the story says so and reads it only as a second record of the Maine keeper. The story now prints the lens conflict as an undated change rather than as a flat contradiction, and gives LighthouseFriends' 1933 next to the archive's 1934.
